checkpoints: Setting a dedup marker before the effect it represents has actually happened turns the marker into a claim about the future rather than a record of the past, so a crash between the claim and the effect leaves the marker orphaned with no matching state.

In this code, `redis.set(dedupKey, "1", "EX", 3600, "NX")` succeeds and returns before `repo.save(row)` is even attempted, so a process crash between those two lines leaves Redis believing the event was handled while Postgres has no row for it.

Because the Kafka offset was never committed when the crash happened, the broker redelivers the exact same message — and on redelivery `processEvent` finds the dedup key already set and throws `ConflictException`, silently discarding the only legitimate attempt to persist that event.

The happy-path tests (first-time processing succeeds, an exact duplicate gets skipped) never exercise a crash landing between the SETNX and the save, which is why the bug survives behind a fully green test suite.

The durable source of truth for "this event was processed" should be the effect itself — the Postgres row, ideally backed by a unique constraint on `clientMessageId` — rather than a cache entry that gets set ahead of that effect actually happening.

A correct restructuring persists the row first (or performs the dedup check and the write inside the same unit of work) and only writes or refreshes the Redis key after the database commit succeeds, turning Redis into a best-effort cache of an already-durable fact instead of a lock claimed in advance.

A smaller patch that doesn't change the ordering is to wrap the persist step in a try/catch and explicitly delete the dedup key on any failure that occurs after the SETNX, so a crash-and-retry sees a clean slate on the next redelivery instead of a stale orphaned key.

The fix can be verified by forcing `repo.save` to throw once, redelivering the same `clientMessageId`, and asserting the retry actually writes the row rather than being skipped as a duplicate, with exactly one row ending up in `processed_events` for that id.
